mstts:express-as.prosody: Welcome. I'm so glad you're here, joining me for a journey that asks some tough, honest questions about race, language, and justice in America. Have you ever wondered how the words we use—especially the ones loaded with history and pain—can shape the very way justice is delivered? Or how identity itself can tip the scales in a courtroom, even when the law claims to be neutral? Together, we're about to explore these ideas through the lens of Jody Armour’s thought-provoking book, N*gga Theory: Race, Language, Unequal Justice, and the Law. This isn’t just about legal theory—it’s about the lived realities of people whose stories often go unheard. We’ll dig deep into how language doesn’t just reflect bias, but can actually reinforce and deepen the inequalities already woven into our justice system. Along the way, we’ll challenge old assumptions about what makes someone “guilty” or “innocent,” and ask who really gets to define right and wrong—and at what cost. Get ready to reconsider what you think you know about blame, punishment, and the line between personal responsibility and systemic oppression. I invite you to keep an open mind as we question how words become weapons, and how rethinking their power might open the door to empathy, understanding, and much-needed reform. So, let’s dive in together and see what new possibilities we can discover at the crossroads of language and justice.

Chapter 1: The Weight of Words and the Burden of Stigma.
You know, it’s so easy to forget just how much language shapes the world around us—especially when it comes to words that can sting, divide, or define who we are.
In some neighborhoods, where every day feels like a negotiation with suspicion, just a single word can carry the weight of a thousand judgments.
Take the N-word, for example. It’s not just a slur or a reclaimed badge—it’s become a symbol of how society sees, judges, and so often condemns Blackness itself.
Picture this: a teenager, walking home with their hoodie up, music in their ears. They’re not thinking about the law, but the law? It’s thinking about them.
Every glance from a neighbor, every sideways look from a patrol car, is filtered through a long history of language that’s marked certain bodies as dangerous, criminal, or somehow less deserving.
The word “n*gga” floats in the air—it might be spat out as an insult, tossed around among friends, or even whispered in courtrooms as supposed evidence of character.
Depending on who’s saying it, and who’s hearing it, it can mean belonging or banishment.
What most people don’t realize is just how deeply the law is tangled up with these words. The criminal justice system doesn’t just punish actions—it punishes identities.
The words in police reports, courtroom arguments, and news stories often draw an invisible line between those presumed innocent, and those presumed guilty.
And for so many, that line’s been drawn with words that have justified exclusion and violence for centuries.
Imagine a young man, sitting at the defendant’s table. His fate hangs on every word picked by lawyers and witnesses.
The prosecutor calls him “menacing,” “uncooperative,” “streetwise.” The defense tries to flip the script with words like “misunderstood,” “hardworking,” “family-oriented.”
But there’s an unspoken word—the one everyone’s thinking, but nobody says aloud—hanging over everything.
It’s the word that’s followed him since childhood, shaping how the jury sees him, making it all too easy to assume he’s guilty.
But this isn’t just about one word. It’s about how language becomes a stand-in for race, for class, for worthiness.
The law likes to claim it’s neutral, but the words it uses? They’re anything but. Each one carries the weight of history, prejudice, and fear.
And for those living under that shadow, justice can feel like a promise that’s always just out of reach.
The power of language to shape legal outcomes isn’t just a theory—it plays out in real courtrooms, in real lives, every single day.
Picture a mother, sitting in the gallery, watching her son’s trial. Every word used to describe him feels like a fresh sting.
She knows he’s more than the labels being thrown around—she’s seen him help his little sister with homework, seen him working late shifts to help with rent.
But the jury? They see the words, and those words start to become the truth.
Over time, it’s become clear: the law’s reliance on language isn’t an accident. It’s a way to maintain control, to keep certain people in their place.
Listen to how Black defendants are described compared to white ones, even when the facts are nearly identical. The law pretends to be blind—but its language tells another story.
For those on the receiving end, the burden is heavy. Every run-in with the legal system is a reminder that words can be weapons, and that justice often depends on who gets to tell the story.
So, the fight for justice isn’t just about changing laws—it’s about changing the language that holds them up.
It’s about refusing to accept the old labels that have justified inequality for far too long.

Chapter 2: How the Law Reinforces Racial Hierarchies
You’ve probably heard it said that the law is supposed to be the great equalizer—everybody gets treated the same, no matter who they are.
But if you’ve ever sat in a courtroom, dealt with the police, or even just gotten pulled over, you know that’s not always how it works.
In reality, the law doesn’t just mirror society’s prejudices—it actually gives them power, making them official.
Think about a young man heading home from work. He gets stopped by the police, and he already knows the drill: keep his hands where they can see them, stay calm, don’t move too fast.
The questions he gets aren’t really about finding out what happened—they’re based on the idea that he’s already guilty.
Officers use words like “suspicious,” “agitated,” or “noncompliant.” These aren’t just harmless descriptions—they’re loaded cues that set the stage for what comes next.
The law takes those words and gives them weight, turning them into reasons for a search, an arrest, or sometimes even something worse.
Most folks don’t see how deep these assumptions run in our legal system.
Rules about who gets stopped, who gets searched, and who ends up facing charges—all of them are shaped by a long history of racial bias.
The law likes to claim it’s “colorblind,” but the facts tell a different story.
Black people are more likely to be arrested, charged with serious crimes, and handed harsher sentences.
Even the way people talk about them—in the media or in court—makes it all too easy to see them as threats, as problems, instead of real people with real lives.
Picture a dad who’s never been in trouble before, suddenly facing charges after a small argument.
The police report calls him “hostile” and “aggressive.”
The prosecutor paints him as violent, someone who can’t be trusted.
When the jury hears these words, it’s easier for them to imagine the worst.
The dad’s own story—his struggles, hopes, and the way he tries to care for his family—gets drowned out.
What’s really happening here?
The law isn’t just punishing actions—it’s punishing identities.
Even when race isn’t mentioned, the language used in courtrooms is full of hidden meanings.
Words like “urban,” “gang-related,” or “at-risk” are just coded ways to say Black, or other, or dangerous.
The law uses this language to draw lines, to decide who counts and who doesn’t.
And it doesn’t stop at the courthouse.
This kind of thinking shapes how entire communities are seen.
Schools, employers, landlords—they all pick up on these cues from the law.
When Blackness gets linked to crime, it’s not just about the risk of arrest—it’s about finding a job, renting a place, or simply walking through the world without being watched.
The law’s words become a kind of prophecy, making the very inequalities it claims to fix even worse.
Lots of people think you can fix this by just changing a few rules—tweak here, reform there.
But as long as the language of the law stays the same, so will the outcomes.
The real challenge?
We have to tackle the ways the law keeps social hierarchies in place.
We need a system that sees people as individuals, not as stereotypes.
For those who’ve been on the receiving end of this, the pain runs deep.
Every run-in with the law is a reminder that justice isn’t just about what you did—it’s about who you are, and how the world chooses to see you.
Until the law learns to speak a new language—one that recognizes everyone’s humanity—real equality will keep slipping out of reach.

Chapter 3: The Power and Peril of Reclaiming Language
Let’s talk about something that’s both powerful and risky—the way some words, especially slurs, get reclaimed and transformed. Think about the N-word. In certain circles, it’s been flipped on its head. What once was meant to hurt now becomes a shield, a way for people to take back a bit of the power that was used against them.
Among close friends, you’ll hear it tossed around like a code—a signal that says, “Hey, I understand your struggle. We’ve survived together.” It’s almost like a badge of belonging, a small gesture that means, “I see you.”
But let’s be real—the word doesn’t always lose its sting. In different places, or when it’s hurled by the wrong person, it can turn right back into a weapon. Just a few blocks away, that same word might be used to tear someone down, to remind them they don’t belong. The meaning isn’t fixed. It changes depending on who’s saying it, who’s listening, and where it’s said.
Here’s something most people don’t realize—so much is at stake in these little moments. Reclaiming a slur can feel empowering, but it’s always a bit of a gamble. Sure, it builds solidarity. But sometimes, it ends up reinforcing the very divisions and hierarchies we’re trying to break.
And when it comes to the law, things get even messier. Courtrooms aren’t built for nuance. The N-word, for example, is often treated as a red flag—evidence that someone’s got a bad character, maybe even criminal intent. Judges and juries can be quick to judge, assuming anyone who uses that word must be dangerous or beyond redemption.
Imagine this—a young woman ends up on trial for something minor. The prosecutor digs up her old text messages, where she’s used the N-word with friends. Suddenly, what was private language among people who get it, is put on public display. The jury doesn’t see the context, just the word. The verdict? Fast, and harsh.
It’s moments like these that show us something deeper: the legal system struggles with reclaimed language. The law likes to pretend words have set meanings, that intent doesn’t matter as much as impact. But if you’ve lived through the sting of slurs, you know—reclaiming them is survival. It’s about refusing to let others define you. And when the law refuses to see that complexity, it creates its own kind of harm.
It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking that banning certain words will fix everything. But that’s not enough. The real challenge? Understanding why those words carry so much weight in the first place. This fight over language is really a fight over whose reality counts, whose stories get told.
The law needs to do more than just silence offensive words. It needs to truly listen—especially to the people who are most affected. Otherwise, it’s missing the point.
For anyone reclaiming the N-word, there’s always a risk. Every time it’s spoken, there’s a chance it’ll be misunderstood, twisted, or even used against you. But there’s hope in the act of reclamation itself—a belief that language can change, and that the pains of the past don’t have to shape our future.

Chapter 4: Stereotypes, Prejudice, and the Reality of Unequal Justice.
Every day, people move through the world carrying the weight of stereotypes they never asked for. For some, these labels might just be a small irritation—something you brush off. But for others, they can mean the difference between freedom and a life forever changed.
Picture this—a young man stands in front of a judge, accused of a crime he swears he didn’t commit. There’s barely any solid evidence, but the prosecutor keeps bringing up his so-called “history”—maybe a few past mistakes, or just being seen with the wrong crowd. The jury listens, and suddenly, they’re not just seeing one person. They’re seeing every story they’ve ever heard about young Black men and crime. The outcome feels like it was decided before the trial even started.
Most of us don’t realize just how deeply these prejudices are woven into our justice system. From the moment someone’s arrested, every choice—whether it’s bail, what charges to file, plea deals, or sentencing—gets colored by silent assumptions. Who looks dangerous? Who seems trustworthy? Who deserves another chance? The law says it’s impartial, but if you look at the outcomes, you’ll see a very different story.
In some neighborhoods, parents give their kids careful instructions: don’t stand out, keep your hands visible when you walk past the police, always be extra careful. They know that one wrong move could change everything. The fear isn’t just about crime—it’s about being seen as a criminal, about getting tangled up in suspicions you can’t shake off.
Over time, it becomes clear: the justice system’s use of stereotypes isn’t just a bug—it’s built into the design. The system sorts people into boxes, making snap judgments about who belongs and who doesn’t. For anyone who even slightly fits the “criminal” profile, justice can seem out of reach before the first word is spoken in court.
It’s easy to fall into the trap of blaming individuals for their own struggles, forgetting how the system sets them up to fail. The real challenge is to take a hard look at the structures that make it so easy to believe the worst about certain people. We should demand a system that digs deeper, that looks past the surface.
For those who carry these labels, the price is heartbreaking. One arrest can lead to losing a job, breaking up families, or seeing dreams slip away. The stigma follows them everywhere, a constant reminder that they’re seen as less than, as untrustworthy or undeserving of compassion.
So, the fight for justice is really a fight against the power of stereotypes—a battle against the lazy thinking that reduces people to problems. It’s about choosing to see each person as an individual and recognizing the humanity that the system so often ignores.
Until our laws learn to look past the labels, to judge each of us by our actions—not our identities—real justice will always feel just out of reach.

Chapter 5: Centering the Voices of the Most Marginalized.
When we talk about criminal justice reform, most of the conversation circles around policy updates, new laws, or better training for officers. But if you’ve ever lived under that constant cloud of suspicion, you know real change is about something much deeper. It’s about finally being seen. It’s about being heard. Most of all, it’s about being treated as fully human.
Picture this: a community gathers in a church basement. The air feels heavy—there’s frustration, but there’s hope, too. One by one, people stand up and share their stories. They talk about losing loved ones to the system, about dreams that vanished after a single mistake. Sure, there’s anger—but there’s also this fierce determination to demand something better.
The conversation shifts. Folks start asking what justice really means—not just for people who are innocent, but for those who’ve messed up, who’ve been treated as if they could never change.
Now, here’s something a lot of people miss: It’s actually pretty rare for the voices of the most marginalized to be at the center of these talks. Too often, reforms get shaped by folks who’ve never felt the sting of a slur, never been eyed suspiciously in a store, never had to justify themselves to a cop. So, you end up with a system that tweaks things around the edges, but never really digs into why injustice happens in the first place.
There’s one story that sticks with me—a man stands up and shares that he spent years in prison for a crime he didn’t commit. He talks about the pain of being branded, the uphill battle to rebuild, and how society still treats him like he’s dangerous. Yet, even with all that, he talks about hope—hope that things can change, that maybe the next generation won’t have to go through what he did.
What really hits home is this: real justice takes more than just passing new laws. It calls for an honest reckoning with what people on the margins face every day. It starts by listening—truly listening—to their stories, learning from what they’ve lived through, and making sure their needs are front and center in every decision.
It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking justice is just about punishing the guilty and protecting the innocent. But it’s more complicated than that. Real justice is about healing. It’s about restoration. It’s about building a world where everyone actually gets a shot at thriving.
For folks who’ve been pushed aside, the struggle doesn’t stop. Every single day, it’s a fight to be noticed, to be heard, to be treated with basic dignity. But there’s real strength in coming together, in refusing to let those old labels define who you are.
The road to justice? It’s long. It’s tough. But it always starts with something simple: listening. Until we put the voices of the most marginalized right at the heart of the conversation, the promise of equal justice is just that—a promise, not a reality.

Chapter 6. The Myth of the “Good Victim” and the Limits of Sympathy.
You ever notice that quiet, unspoken rule in our justice system? It’s like—only a certain kind of victim really gets our sympathy. The law, and the folks who make it, draw these invisible lines between people they believe deserve compassion, and those they don’t. And if you’re on the wrong side of that line? You’re often left standing alone, unheard, and unprotected.
Imagine a mother whose son has been shot. She stands in front of a crowd, her grief so raw you can almost feel it. But instead of comfort, she’s bombarded with questions about her son—what kind of friends did he have, what choices did he make, what music did he listen to? The message is pretty clear: if he wasn’t perfect, maybe he somehow brought this on himself.
The legal system? It asks those same questions, digging for reasons to hold back empathy.
Most folks don’t even realize how this logic slips into every part of the system. When a Black person is harmed, the first reaction is often to look for flaws—to find some reason to question their innocence. This whole idea of the “good victim” becomes a shield for keeping things just as they are. It lets us avoid facing the deeper roots of violence and injustice.
Think about a young woman who’s been assaulted. She hesitates to call the police, already knowing her own record will be thrown back in her face. And when she finally does reach out, the officers seem more interested in her past than in what happened to her. Suddenly, the courtroom isn’t a place for healing—it’s a place where her pain gets weighed against her mistakes, where her worthiness is constantly under scrutiny.
You start to realize that the law’s sympathy only goes out to those who fit a narrow mold. The rest? They’re left to fend for themselves, their suffering brushed off as just the price of poor choices. But this isn’t just a lack of empathy—it’s a failure of justice.
It’s so easy to fall into the trap of thinking only the blameless deserve help. But here’s something to remember: everyone carries scars. Everyone’s made mistakes. If justice only shows up for perfection, then almost nobody gets real justice. The real challenge is creating a system that sees the full humanity in every person, no matter what’s in their past.
For those denied sympathy, that pain doesn’t just fade after the verdict. It sticks with them—a sharp reminder that, to the law, some lives seem to matter more than others.
So, the fight for justice? It’s really about expanding our circle of care. It’s about seeing the dignity in every single story.
Because until the law learns to offer compassion without conditions, the promise of equal justice is always going to feel a little bit empty.

Chapter 7: The Double Bind—Respectability and Survival.
There’s a pressure that hums just beneath the surface for so many people living under constant suspicion—the need to appear “respectable.” Have you ever felt like you have to play by invisible rules just to stay out of trouble? For some, that’s not just a feeling. It’s a survival strategy. You do everything right, or at least you try, just to prove you’re not like the stereotypes.
But here’s the catch: it’s a trap. It means living with constant vigilance, always worried that even the smallest misstep could cost you everything.
Imagine a teenager—he keeps his head down, dresses neatly, speaks softly. He’s been taught this is how to stay safe, how to make sure nobody sees him as a threat. But then one day, he gets stopped by the police anyway. The officers don’t care about his good grades or his polite manners. They only see what they expect to see. And the lesson hits hard: no matter how respectable he tries to be, suspicion still follows him.
Most people don’t realize just how exhausting it is to live this way. Every choice—what you wear, how you speak, even where you go—is shaped by a fear of being misunderstood or misread. And the law? It tends to reward those who fit a certain mold and punish those who don’t. But let’s be honest: the mold is nearly impossible for most people to fit, especially when the rules seem to change all the time.
Take the story of a young woman denied a job because of her criminal record, even after years of hard work and giving back to her community. She’s told she has to “prove herself,” but no matter what she does, her past keeps following her. The respectability society demands always seems just out of reach.
What’s really going on here? The double bind of respectability and survival is actually a form of control. It keeps people on edge, always striving for approval that never really comes. The law uses this bind to justify leaving people out, to blame inequality on the individual instead of the system itself.
Many folks end up blaming themselves for not measuring up. But let’s be clear—the standards are designed to be impossible. The real challenge? It’s rejecting the lie that your worth depends on being perfect, and demanding a system that values you for who you are.
For those caught in this double bind, it’s about more than just missed opportunities. It’s the constant stress, the feeling that you’re never quite enough, and the fear that one mistake could wipe out years of effort. The fight for justice is really a fight to break free from these impossible demands—to build a world where survival doesn’t depend on respectability.
Until the law learns to look past the surface and truly see the humanity in every struggle, real justice will always be just out of reach.

Chapter 8. The Law’s Blind Spots: Intent, Context, and Humanity.
You know, the law likes to picture itself as this precise, objective thing—always fair, always clear. But if you’ve ever looked closely, you’ll notice something’s missing. In its search for certainty, the law often overlooks the real, messy stuff that makes us human.
Think about intent and context. What someone meant to do, what they were actually going through at the time—that often gets swept aside for a simple label: guilty or not guilty, criminal or innocent.
Imagine a man who lashes out in a moment of fear. The law, in its black-and-white view, sees only the action—not the years of pain or trauma that led him there. In court, everything he’s lived through gets boiled down into a few dry lines on a police report. The prosecutor zeroes in on the facts. The defense tries to fill in the blanks. But really, the whole system is designed to ignore the gray areas.
Most people don’t realize just how much gets lost when context disappears. The language of the law? It’s rigid. Its categories don’t leave much room for real life—life that’s full of nuance, hope, pain, and contradiction. And when the system shuts out that complexity, people get turned into one-dimensional characters. Their real stories are flattened, sometimes beyond recognition.
Take this example—a mother accused of neglect because she left her kids alone to go to work. The law just sees a crime. But her neighbors? They see a mom doing everything she can in a situation that’s almost impossible. Suddenly, the courtroom turns into a battlefield where rules clash with reality, and understanding gets pushed aside.
What’s striking is that these blind spots aren’t just random mistakes. They’re built in. By ignoring intent and context, the law keeps up the appearance of fairness, but often ends up fueling injustice. And it’s the people whose lives don’t fit into neat little boxes who get hurt the most.
It’s easy to slip into thinking that justice is only about following the rules. But here’s something to pay attention to: rules without understanding can cause as much harm as good. The real challenge? Building a system that sees the whole person—that recognizes every story’s complexity.
For anyone who’s been misjudged, the consequences stick. One moment can shape an entire lifetime, and the chance for a second act is slim. That’s why the fight for justice really means fighting to bring humanity back into the system, and insisting that context and intent matter.
Until the law learns to see people in all their fullness, real justice will always feel just out of reach.

Chapter 9: Radical Imagination—Rethinking Justice from the Ground Up.
Sometimes, the only way forward is to imagine something completely new. If you've ever felt let down by the system, you know that just tweaking things a bit isn't enough. What we really need is a radical reimagining—a bold willingness to ask, "What would justice look like if it truly served everyone?"
Picture this—a community center filled with people, all dreaming out loud together. They're talking about safety that doesn't depend on surveillance, real accountability that doesn't mean punishment, and healing without shame or humiliation. The ideas might be bold—sometimes even a little messy—but they’re always grounded in the belief that another world is possible.
Most people don’t realize just how powerful imagination can be. The law often feels set in stone, like there’s no way around it. But every rule was made by people—and that means every rule can be changed. The first real step? It’s listening to those who’ve been hurt the most, and letting their visions lead the way.
Let me share a story. There’s a group of folks who were formerly incarcerated. They started a program to help others coming home from prison. They offer rides, job training, or sometimes just a listening ear. The work is tough, and the resources are limited, but the impact? It’s real. For everyone involved, it’s a glimpse of what justice could be—not just punishing, but restoring.
It becomes clear that radical imagination isn’t just about dreaming big—it’s about getting to work. It means refusing to accept the limits of the current system and insisting that dignity and safety can be within reach for everyone.
It’s easy to fall into the habit of thinking change is impossible, that the system is just too massive to challenge. But here’s the truth—every movement for justice started with someone daring to imagine something better. The real challenge is keeping that hope alive, turning vision into action.
For people who’ve been told they don’t belong, radical imagination becomes a lifeline. It’s a way to take back agency, to demand a future where every life is honored. The fight for justice is really a fight to make what seems impossible, possible.
And until the law learns how to dream, right alongside the people it’s harmed, justice will always be unfinished business.

Chapter 10: The Ongoing Struggle — Hope, Resistance, and the Work Ahead.
Change almost never happens overnight, does it? For folks who’ve spent years fighting for justice, the road can feel endless—and honestly, pretty lonely at times. Still, there’s something powerful in those small victories, in moments of connection and courage. That’s where hope hangs on.
Picture this—a father walks his daughter to school, his grip tightening just a bit as they pass a police car. He’s all too aware of the dangers out there, but he also trusts in the strength of his community. Every day, he’s teaching her to stand tall, to speak her mind, and to truly believe in her own worth.
Most people don’t see the quiet acts of resistance that unfold daily. Think about the neighbor who checks in on kids after school, the teacher who refuses to give up on a struggling student, or the advocate who’s always present—no matter how many court dates pile up. Sure, these moments might not make the headlines, but they’re the real building blocks of lasting change.
Here’s one story that stands out—a group of mothers decide enough is enough after a string of police stops in their neighborhood. They gather, organize a march, hold up their signs, chant together, and demand answers. It’s a small march, but the message echoes loud and clear: “We’re here. We won’t be silent.”
What becomes clear is this—the fight for justice isn’t just about laws or policies. It’s about people. It’s about the relationships that hold us up, and the courage to keep moving, especially when the odds feel stacked against us. The work is tough. Setbacks happen. But that hope? It’s real, and it keeps us going.
It’s so easy to slip into despair, to start thinking nothing will ever change. But here’s something to remember—every act of resistance matters. The real challenge is to keep showing up, to keep believing that something better is possible.
For those who’ve been in this fight for generations, the struggle is both a heavy burden and a unique blessing. It’s a reminder that justice isn’t a finish line—it’s a journey. And that journey belongs to all of us.
Until the law truly learns to honor the resilience of those it’s tried to break, justice will always be a work in progress.

As we wrap up, let’s take a moment to remember what this journey has really been about. Language, race, and justice—they aren’t just abstract ideas or lines in a book. They’re lived out by real people, every single day. It’s in the choices we make, the courage we show, and the hope we hold onto, especially when things feel tough or uncertain.
So, what are the big lessons to carry forward? First, language shapes so much—how the law sees us, how it judges, how it punishes. Stereotypes and the pressure to fit into some narrow idea of respectability? Those are just tools of control, not true justice. When the law ignores context or intent, it ends up causing more harm and keeps people out. Real justice listens first. It centers the voices and needs of the people most often pushed aside. And lasting change? It’s planted by bold imagination and those everyday acts of resistance that, over time, reshape what’s possible.
Here’s what this means for you: The business of justice isn’t locked away in courtrooms or government buildings. It happens in living rooms, in classrooms, around kitchen tables, and out in our communities. It’s there every time someone pushes back against a label, every time a story gets told in full, every time we choose to stand with someone instead of looking away. The road ahead won’t always be obvious, and yes, there will be challenges. But you’re not walking it alone. Every act of listening, every show of empathy, every time you see the whole person behind the headline—that’s how we build a more just world, one step at a time.
So, as you go forward, keep these lessons close. Speak up when language divides. Don’t let stereotypes slide by unnoticed. Listen closely to those whose voices are too often overlooked. And above all, keep imagining what justice could look like if it truly included everyone. The journey is long—but together, step by step, we can bring that vision closer to reality.
